messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Psychologist
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Chukwu's Vigil

Chukwu Okafor was thirty-seven when he came to the clinic on a Tuesday afternoon in October, moving through the waiting room with the deliberate stillness of someone who has learned to take up as little space as possible. He chose a seat with clear sightlines to the door and positioned himself so his back touched the wall. The receptionist had offered him coffee; he declined, explaining that he preferred to keep his hands free. It was the kind of detail most people would not have noticed. It was the kind of detail that had become automatic for him.

Six years earlier, on a night that had reorganized everything that came after it, Chukwu had been locked in a bathroom by a man he had trusted—a colleague from a research conference, someone who had seemed interested in continuing a professional conversation back at the hotel. The man had forced him against the tile, had pinned him there while the lock clicked shut behind them. For Chukwu, the lock had become the punctuation mark of his unmade life. That sound—the definitive metal slide—had become the sound of his body ceasing to belong to him.

For the first months afterward, Chukwu had told no one. He had returned to his private practice in Seattle, where he saw patients with anxiety and depression, where he sat in a comfortable leather chair and helped other people untangle the threads of their suffering. He had kept his back to the wall even then, though he had told himself it was just a preference. By the second year, he had stopped scheduling clients in the afternoon because the light through the windows made him feel exposed, as though the trauma itself were visible on his skin, legible to anyone who looked at him long enough. He had come to believe that people could see it—that some essential damage was written across his face, that his patients must sense it even as he guided them through their own reckonings with fear.

The locked spaces had become impossible first. He had stopped using the bathroom at work, timing his day around trips home. He had declined invitations to conferences, to seminars, to anywhere that might involve a hotel room or a closed door he could not control. When a male colleague from his practice had asked to discuss a difficult case, Chukwu had felt his body go rigid with something beyond caution—a certainty that being alone with another man in a room was a kind of repetition he could not survive again. He had suggested they meet at a coffee shop instead, and the colleague had seemed puzzled, but Chukwu could not explain. How could he say that the presence of another man's body in a confined space had become synonymous with the loss of his own?

Sleep had become an act of resistance. Chukwu would lie in bed, acutely aware that his eyes were closing, that his vigilance was slipping, and he would force himself awake. To sleep was to be defenseless. To sleep was to return to that bathroom, to the moment when he could not see what was happening to his own body. He had installed motion-sensor lights throughout his apartment. He had arranged his furniture so that he could see from his bed to his front door. He had become, in essence, a man who was never quite asleep and never quite awake—existing in a thin, exhausted space between the two.

By the time he called the clinic, Chukwu had not slept more than three hours in a single night in four years. His practice had dwindled; he had referred out most of his clients, telling himself it was time to focus on his own research. What he could not articulate was that sitting across from vulnerable people, holding space for their pain, had become impossible when he could not hold space for his own body. He had come to believe that he had no future—that this state of perpetual readiness, this inability to relax even in the locked safety of his own apartment, was permanent. That nothing could stop what had already happened to him, and therefore nothing could stop it from happening again.

What had finally brought him to seek help was a moment of such profound isolation that it had cracked something open. A friend had invited him to a dinner party. Chukwu had arrived, scanned the room for exits, positioned himself near the kitchen counter. Midway through the evening, someone had made a casual comment about a news story—a case of sexual assault in the city. Chukwu had felt the words land on him like a physical blow. He had excused himself, gone to the bathroom, and sat on the closed toilet lid for twenty minutes, unable to move. When he emerged, he had left without explanation.

Sitting now in the clinic, his back against the wall, Chukwu was hoping that someone could help him understand why his body had decided that the world was a place where he could never be safe again. He was terrified that nothing could change what had happened, and equally terrified of what it would mean if it could.
